official_title: Shall the Charter of the City and County of Denver be amended to expressly clarify that the Auditor's Office may continue to enforce wage laws, worker protection laws, and other workplace rights laws in accordance with ordinances passed by City Council?
plain_summary: Writes into the city charter that the Denver Auditor's Office enforces wage and workplace laws (minimum wage, wage theft, prevailing wage, paid sick leave) when City Council tells it to by ordinance. The Auditor already does this work; the measure makes the charter say so.
yes_means: The charter is updated to state that the Auditor enforces wage and workplace-rights laws as Council requires by ordinance.
no_means: The charter stays as is; the Auditor keeps enforcing wage laws under existing ordinances, but the charter does not spell out that duty.
current_law: The Auditor has enforced Denver's prevailing wage ordinance since 1950. Council added minimum wage and wage theft enforcement in 2016, complaint-based minimum wage enforcement in 2020, and proactive investigations in 2022. The charter's list of Auditor duties does not currently name wage enforcement; it relies on a catch-all 'other duties assigned by ordinance' clause.
fiscal_impact: City Department of Finance: no anticipated fiscal impact, because the Auditor's Office already performs this function.
confusing_wording_note: The question says 'may continue to enforce,' which sounds like the enforcement might stop without it. It won't. A NO vote does not end wage enforcement; it leaves the charter's wording unchanged. Supporters say the amendment 'does not expand the Auditor's Office's authority.' Note the Denver Democrats' page labels this 'Auditor Oversight and Subpoena Authority,' but the ballot text and official booklet say nothing about subpoenas.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say the Auditor's Office has collected about $10 million in restitution and enforced the rights of more than 15,000 workers in the last decade, and that putting the duty in the charter removes any legal uncertainty about the city's enforcement authority. They call it a good-governance cleanup that aligns the charter with existing law and practice.

opponents_case.text: No comments were submitted against this measure to the official Ballot Information Booklet, and the League of Women Voters of Denver reports no known opposition.

official_title: Shall the Charter of the City and County of Denver be amended to adjust the City and County's budget and appropriation process, and in connection therewith, allowing the City Council to adopt a two-year budget planning and adoption process and modernizing or repealing certain charter sections?
plain_summary: Changes how Denver builds its budget. It lets City Council choose (by ordinance) a two-year budget instead of the current one-year budget, moves the Mayor's proposed budget up to the first Friday in September, requires a public input process reported by the third Monday in July, and forces budget-cut plans when spending runs 2% over or revenue 5% under projections. It does not require a two-year budget; Council would still have to vote to adopt one.
yes_means: Council gains the option of a two-year budget cycle, budget deadlines move earlier, a public-input step is added, and automatic budget-reduction triggers kick in when revenue or spending miss projections.
no_means: Denver keeps its current annual budget process and calendar.
current_law: The charter sets a one-year budget. Agencies submit estimates by July 1, the Mayor briefs Council by September 15, proposes a budget by the third Monday in October, and Council adopts it by its second regular November meeting. State law requires Denver to pass a balanced budget every year.
fiscal_impact: City Budget and Management Office: about $50,000 in one-time costs to reconfigure budget software for a two-year term ($30,000 for the budget development system, $20,000 for the publishing system). No cost to move the proposed-budget date earlier.
confusing_wording_note: The title says 'allowing' a two-year budget, not requiring one. Even if 2I passes, Council must separately pass an ordinance by January 31 of the year before a two-year term starts, and the second year still gets its own annual appropriation and a mid-cycle review. The phrase 'modernizing or repealing certain charter sections' hides the other real changes: earlier deadlines, a required public-engagement process, and the 2% and 5% budget-reduction triggers. The ballot question does not mention any of those.

supporters_case.text: Sponsoring council members say a two-year option lets the city and its partners plan long-term projects, frees staff time in year two for program evaluation, adds a required community-input process, gives Council and the public more time to review the budget, and builds in triggers so projected spending cannot outrun revenue by large amounts. Denver could still use a one-year budget in uncertain times.

opponents_case.text: Opponents in the official booklet say Denver 'rarely gets a one-year budget right,' pointing to last year's mid-year $200 million deficit, and that forecasting a general fund that is 56% sales tax two or three years out 'will be wildly off.' They argue a two-year budget hands too much of Council's power of the purse to the Mayor, that the city already uses multi-year contracts and a six-year capital plan, and that more governments are moving away from biennial budgets than toward them.

official_title: Shall the Charter of the City and County of Denver be amended to modernize the Civil Service Commission and Department of Safety by removing outdated language, giving City Council the ability to add duties via code, and providing for an extension of probation when required for medical, military, or other approved leave?
plain_summary: Updates the charter sections that govern hiring, promotion and discipline for Denver police and firefighters. It moves operational details from the charter into city code (so Council can change them without a public vote), removes the caps on police and fire command staff (currently 18 police and 7 fire command assignments), lets probation be extended when a new officer takes medical or military leave, drops the citizenship requirement to serve on the Civil Service Commission, moves the public safety cadet program under the Manager of Safety, updates timelines for disciplinary review, and makes the language gender-neutral.
yes_means: The charter is rewritten as described; Council would then pass an ordinance moving the operational details into city code.
no_means: The current charter rules for the Civil Service Commission, including the command-staff caps and existing probation and discipline timelines, stay in place.
current_law: The Civil Service Commission (five civilian commissioners) runs the merit system for police and fire hiring, promotion and disciplinary appeals under charter rules that date to 1904 and have been amended piecemeal. The charter caps fire command assignments at 7 and police command assignments at 18, requires commissioners to be citizens, and fixes probation and discipline timelines.
fiscal_impact: City Department of Finance: removing the command-staff caps would have a 'de minimis' financial impact if authorized strength does not change; any increase in command staff would be decided by city leaders based on need. Command staff historically get the same raises as the bargaining unit.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot question says 'removing outdated language' and 'giving City Council the ability to add duties via code,' but does not mention the most concrete change: deleting the numeric caps on police and fire command positions. It also does not mention removing the citizenship requirement for commissioners or extending disciplinary timelines. Read 'modernize' as 'move the detailed rules out of the charter so they can be changed by ordinance.'

supporters_case.text: Supporters call it 'a modernization measure, not an overhaul.' They say the 1904-era rules no longer match operations, that moving details to code allows routine adjustments without a charter election, that removing command caps gives departments flexibility as the city grows, and that letting probation pause for approved leave is fair to new hires.

opponents_case.text: No comments were submitted against this measure to the official Ballot Information Booklet, and the League of Women Voters of Denver reports no known opposition. Context: in 2025 the Civil Service Commission's executive director was fired after alleging hiring standards had been lowered, which is the background some critics cite when discussing changes to the commission.

official_title: Shall the City and County of Denver approve the terms of a twenty-year franchise contract, starting January 1, 2027, with Public Service Company of Colorado (Xcel Energy) to continue its program for undergrounding overhead electrical lines, maintaining infrastructure safety, and partnering with the City for emergency management coordination, and to require that Xcel Energy continue to pay the City for reasonable use of public rights-of-way and other City property necessary to provide safe and reliable utility services for the benefit of the City, its residents, and its businesses?
plain_summary: Approves a new 20-year deal (2027 to 2046) letting Xcel Energy keep using Denver's streets and public property for its electric and gas lines. In exchange Xcel keeps paying a 3% franchise fee (about $32 to $34 million a year, which Xcel passes through to Denver customers on their bills), sets aside about $10 million a year to bury overhead power lines where the city directs, and pays to move its lines when city projects require it. The current deal expires December 31, 2026. The charter requires a public vote on any franchise.
yes_means: Denver signs the 20-year franchise and companion partnership agreement with Xcel starting January 1, 2027.
no_means: The current franchise expires at the end of 2026 with no replacement; Xcel would still be required by state law to serve Denver, but the city and Xcel would have to negotiate (and possibly litigate) utility relocations project by project, and the franchise fee's future is disputed.
current_law: Denver has had a franchise with Xcel (and its predecessors) since 1947; the current 20-year agreement runs through December 31, 2026 and charges a 3% franchise fee on Xcel's Denver electric and gas revenues. The existing contract says that if the franchise is not renewed, Xcel must keep paying an amount equal to the fee as long as it uses city rights-of-way; a former PUC chairman disputes whether Xcel could legally keep collecting it from customers. City Council voted 7-6 in 2025 against sending an earlier version to voters, then renegotiated after a working group process.
fiscal_impact: City Department of Finance: franchise fee revenue projected at about $34.3 million in 2027 (plus a one-time $2.5 million payment for utility assistance), of which $2 million a year goes to the Energy Efficiency Assistance Fund and the rest to the General Fund. Over 20 years the city projects $808 million to $902 million in total fees depending on growth. Separately, an estimated $150 million a year in utility relocation costs that Xcel covers under a franchise, and about $10 million a year (1% of electric revenue) that Xcel holds and spends on undergrounding at the city's direction. The fee does not increase; it stays at 3%.
confusing_wording_note: The question is written as a list of benefits ('undergrounding,' 'safety,' 'emergency management,' 'require that Xcel Energy continue to pay the City'). What you are actually voting on is a 20-year contract giving Xcel access to public property. Two things are easy to miss: the 3% 'franchise fee' Xcel 'pays the City' shows up on your utility bill, because state rules let Xcel recover it from Denver customers; and voting NO does not end Xcel service, but it does end the contract on December 31, 2026 with no clear replacement. The opponents' main argument (shorter term, more affordability money, keep public-power options open) is not reflected anywhere in the ballot language, and no one filed a for or against statement in the official booklet.

supporters_case.text: The Johnston administration and the Yes on 2K campaign say the deal is 'a better deal for Denver than it is for Xcel': it locks in about $32 million a year for the General Fund, saves the city an estimated $150 million a year in relocation costs, funds undergrounding, adds a $2.5 million bill-assistance payment and $125,000 a year for income-qualified programs, lets Denver intervene in rate cases, and creates a community advisory structure. Without it the city would pay Xcel to move lines for its own projects.

opponents_case.text: Opponents (Together Colorado, Denver DSA, and critics summarized by LWV Denver) say the affordability money is small next to rising bills, that undergrounding funds may not reach the neighborhoods most in need without enforceable criteria, that 20 years is too long given climate goals and rate hikes, and that signing makes municipal power or other public-ownership options less likely. DSA wants the city to 'force Xcel back to the bargaining table' for a shorter deal.

official_title: Shall the voters of the City and County of Denver adopt an ordinance prohibiting the force-feeding of birds and, in connection therewith, prohibiting the sale of products derived from force-feeding birds, including foie gras?
plain_summary: Bans force-feeding birds in Denver and bans restaurants and stores from selling, importing or distributing foie gras and other 'fattened bird liver products' made from force-fed ducks or geese. Fines run $1,000 to $5,000 per violation per day, with a mandatory license suspension of up to six months for repeat violations within 12 months. Denver's health department would enforce it starting July 1, 2027. Personal possession and eating are not restricted. Veterinarians may tube-feed sick birds.
yes_means: Starting July 1, 2027, no one may force-feed birds in Denver or sell force-fed bird liver products (foie gras and similar) in Denver.
no_means: No change; Denver restaurants and stores may keep selling foie gras.
current_law: No Denver or Colorado law restricts force-feeding birds or selling foie gras. No foie gras is produced in Denver; some Denver restaurants serve it. California, New York City, Pittsburgh, Portland and Washington, D.C. have bans (D.C. voters also decide one this November).
fiscal_impact: City Department of Finance, after consulting the Department of Public Health and Environment: no anticipated fiscal impact; any added workload is minimal and absorbed by existing inspectors.
confusing_wording_note: The question reads like it is only about 'force-feeding,' which no one does in Denver. The real effect is the sales ban: restaurants and grocers could not sell foie gras, duck-liver pâté or similar products. Two definitions are broader than the headline: 'fattened bird liver products' includes 'duck fat, pâtés, spreads, cured products' derived from fattened livers, and 'bird' covers all poultry. The penalties ($1,000 to $5,000 per day, license suspension for repeat violations) are not in the ballot question.

supporters_case.text: Pro-Animal Colorado and the volunteer-led campaign say force-feeding ducks and geese until their livers swell to ten times normal size is 'cruel and unnecessary,' that foie gras is a luxury item sold as a seasonal dish rather than a revenue source for any business, that enforcement costs almost nothing because inspections already happen, and that a CSU poll found 85% of Colorado voters support ending sales from force-feeding farms.

opponents_case.text: No comments were submitted against this measure to the official booklet. The League of Women Voters of Denver summarizes the arguments against: limits on what restaurants may serve restrict independent creativity, add regulatory burden and cost to small businesses, and will not stop anyone from eating foie gras since they can dine in a neighboring city.

official_title: SHALL DENVER PUBLIC SCHOOLS (SCHOOL DISTRICT NO. 1) TAXES BE INCREASED UP TO $44 MILLION IN 2026 (FOR COLLECTION IN 2027) AND ANNUALLY THEREAFTER FOR EDUCATIONAL PURPOSES, INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO: INCREASING EDUCATOR PAY; OFFERING STUDENTS MORE CAREER AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION COURSES IN HIGH DEMAND FIELDS; STUDENT MENTAL HEALTH AND SPECIAL EDUCATION; WITH ALL SPENDING OF SUCH REVENUES REPORTED IN THE DISTRICT'S ANNUAL INDEPENDENT AUDIT PUBLISHED ON THE DISTRICT'S WEBSITE; BY THE IMPOSITION OF A MILL LEVY THAT, WHEN COMBINED WITH OTHER MILL LEVY OVERRIDES APPROVED BY DENVER VOTERS FOR THE DISTRICT'S GENERAL FUND, EQUALS THE AMOUNT PERMITTED BY SECTION 22-54-108(3)(B)(VI), BY THE LEVY OF PROPERTY TAXES AT A RATE SUFFICIENT TO PRODUCE SUCH AMOUNTS; WHICH TAXES SHALL BE DEPOSITED INTO THE GENERAL FUND OF THE DISTRICT AND SHALL BE IN ADDITION TO THE PROPERTY TAXES THAT OTHERWISE WOULD BE LEVIED FOR THE GENERAL FUND; AND SHALL INVESTMENT EARNINGS ON THE PROCEEDS OF SUCH TAXES BE TREATED AS A VOTER-APPROVED REVENUE CHANGE UNDER ARTICLE X, SECTION 20 OF THE COLORADO CONSTITUTION?
plain_summary: A property tax increase (a 'mill levy override') of about 4 mills that raises $44 million a year for Denver Public Schools, every year, with no end date. DPS plans to spend $25.8 million on a flat $1,750 raise for every full-time employee (prorated for part-time), $4 million on career and technical education, $2.9 million on student mental health, $2 million on special education, and $9.3 million passed to DPS charter schools as state law requires. Cost: about $11.50 a year per $100,000 of home value, or about $72 a year on the median Denver home ($624,800).
yes_means: DPS property taxes rise by up to $44 million a year starting with taxes collected in 2027, for the purposes listed.
no_means: DPS property tax rates stay as they are; no new override revenue.
current_law: Denver voters last approved a DPS mill levy override in 2020 ($32 million) and a $975 million bond in 2024. Colorado's TABOR requires voter approval for any tax increase, and state law caps total overrides at a share of the district's program funding (C.R.S. 22-54-108(3)(b)(VI)). Overrides pay for operations such as salaries; bonds can only pay for buildings and equipment. DPS enrollment is declining, which reduces state per-pupil funding.
fiscal_impact: TABOR notice: maximum $44,000,000 in the first full fiscal year (2026-27). DPS estimates 2026-27 spending of $1,732,617,232 without the increase, up 18.12% from 2022-23. Supporters' estimate: $11.50 per $100,000 of home value per year.
confusing_wording_note: TABOR requires the title to start 'SHALL ... TAXES BE INCREASED' in all caps, which looks alarming but is standard. 'Up to $44 million in 2026 (for collection in 2027)' means the first bill arrives in early 2027. 'Annually thereafter' means it is permanent unless voters repeal it. The spending list says 'including, but not limited to,' so the three named priorities are not legally binding allocations; the $1,750 raise is a board plan, not ballot text. About $9.3 million of the $44 million goes to charter schools by state law, which the ballot does not mention.

supporters_case.text: DPS, the Denver Classroom Teachers Association and the Yes on 4A committee say a $1,750 base raise for all staff, including bus drivers, custodians and food service workers, keeps DPS competitive with surrounding districts as housing and health costs outpace pay; that $4 million funds programming for the career and technical education hubs built with the 2024 bond; and that $5 million adds counselors, mental health staff and special education support. 'The cost to homeowners is modest and predictable.'

opponents_case.text: No comments against were filed with the TABOR notice by the deadline. The Denver Gazette editorial board urges NO, saying DPS 'has lost the confidence of the public and can't be trusted with the extra money' after years of board feuding. LWV Denver summarizes opponents: property taxes have already risen sharply (statewide collections from $7.18 billion in 2015 to $15.3 billion in 2024), people risk being taxed out of their homes, and results have not matched spending.

jurisdiction: Front Range Passenger Rail District (13 Front Range counties, including Denver, Arapahoe, Jefferson and Adams)
official_title: SHALL FRONT RANGE PASSENGER RAIL DISTRICT TAXES BE INCREASED $295,000,000 ANNUALLY AND BY WHATEVER AMOUNTS ARE RAISED ANNUALLY THEREAFTER, AND SHALL FRONT RANGE PASSENGER RAIL DISTRICT DEBT BE INCREASED $580,000,000, WITH A REPAYMENT COST OF $785,000,000; TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE, AND MAINTAIN COLORADO CONNECTOR (COCO) PASSENGER RAIL SERVICE ON COLORADO'S FRONT RANGE AND CONNECT COMMUNITIES, INCLUDING PUEBLO, COLORADO SPRINGS, STERLING RANCH, LITTLETON, DENVER, WESTMINSTER, BROOMFIELD, LOUISVILLE, BOULDER, LONGMONT, LOVELAND, AND FORT COLLINS; IN ORDER TO: REMOVE VEHICLES FROM HIGHWAYS AND INCREASE TRAVEL CAPACITY; CONNECT TRAVELERS TO EMPLOYMENT CENTERS, COLLEGES, SPORTS ARENAS, AND ENTERTAINMENT HUBS ALONG THE FRONT RANGE; AND INVEST IN STATION AREA IMPROVEMENTS AND LOCAL CONNECTIONS TO RAIL STATIONS; BY ESTABLISHING A 0.333% SALES AND USE TAX (EQUAL TO ONE THIRD OF A PENNY ON A $1 PURCHASE), WITH EXEMPTIONS PROVIDED UNDER COLORADO LAW, INCLUDING THOSE FOR GASOLINE, FOOD, RESIDENTIAL ELECTRICITY AND GAS, PRESCRIPTION DRUGS, AND MEDICAL SUPPLIES; AND TO RETAIN ALL SUCH REVENUES, PUBLIC AND PRIVATE CONTRIBUTIONS, AND ANY INVESTMENT INCOME ON REVENUES AND DEBT PROCEEDS, AS A VOTER-APPROVED REVENUE CHANGE UNDER SECTION 20 OF ARTICLE X OF THE COLORADO CONSTITUTION; AND REQUIRING THAT ALL SUCH DEDICATED REVENUES BE REVIEWED ANNUALLY BY AN INDEPENDENT AUDITOR AND A ROTATING GROUP OF CITIZEN TAXPAYERS WHO LIVE IN THE DISTRICT?
plain_summary: A new 0.333% sales tax (33 cents on $100) across 13 Front Range counties to build and run the 'Colorado Connector' (CoCo) passenger train from Pueblo through Colorado Springs, Denver and Boulder to Fort Collins, plus up to $580 million in borrowing. Groceries, gas, home utilities and medicine are exempt. Denver voters are in the district, so this is on every Denver ballot. It is a regional measure, not a Denver measure, and passes or fails on the combined vote of the whole district.
yes_means: The 0.333% sales tax starts, the district may borrow up to $580 million, and the money goes to building and operating Front Range passenger rail.
no_means: No new sales tax; the district keeps planning with existing state funds but has no dedicated local revenue to build the line.
current_law: The legislature created the Front Range Passenger Rail District in 2021 with authority to ask voters for a sales tax of up to 0.8%. The state has spent more than $300 million on planning and related work. No dedicated tax exists today. Some service between Denver and the north is planned to start on existing freight tracks; the full Pueblo-to-Fort Collins line would take years to build.
fiscal_impact: Ballot title: up to $295 million a year in new tax, $580 million in debt with a $785 million repayment cost. The exact fiscal notice is in the district's TABOR notice mailed to voters in the 13 counties; the Denver notice includes it on the ballot but Denver's own TABOR mailer covers only 4A.
pass_threshold: simple majority of all voters in the 13-county district combined
confusing_wording_note: Two things trip people up. First, 'TAXES BE INCREASED $295,000,000 ANNUALLY AND BY WHATEVER AMOUNTS ARE RAISED ANNUALLY THEREAFTER' is TABOR's required format; it means the first-year estimate is $295 million and later years float with sales. Second, a printing error put 7A on about 800,000 ballots in Adams, Arapahoe, Douglas and Weld counties for voters who live outside the district. The state's guidance is: do not request a replacement; clerks will hand-review and set aside ineligible 7A votes. Denver ballots are correct; every Denver voter is in the district. If you live in Aurora, Lakewood, Englewood or Thornton, you may or may not be in the district depending on your exact address; vote it anyway and the clerk will sort it out.

supporters_case.text: Supporters (the district, Colorado Rail Passenger Association, Bell Policy Center, LWV Denver, Denver Democrats) say the train would take cars off I-25, connect job centers, colleges and stadiums, and that the tax is small and exempts necessities. Bell Policy Center calls it a long-needed investment in a corridor where highway widening cannot keep up with growth.

opponents_case.text: The Denver Gazette editorial board calls it 'a white elephant on rails,' arguing it will not relieve I-25 traffic and that the state's $300 million already spent 'would have been better spent on our highways.' Opponents have also asked that the measure be thrown out because of the ballot printing error in four counties.

official_title: Shall the City of Aurora raise the sales and use tax rate by 0.129% starting on Jan. 1, 2027, to provide for the operation of and repairs, maintenance and improvements to community facilities, including without limitation libraries, recreation and community centers... (ballot language as quoted by the Denver Gazette from Aurora's ballot information site; full TABOR title not captured)
plain_summary: A new 0.129% Aurora sales tax (about 13 cents on $100) from 2027 through 2057, and up to $105 million in bonds, for libraries, recreation centers and parks. One of three companion tax questions (3A, 3B, 3C) that together would raise Aurora's sales tax by 0.325%, the city's first sales tax increase since 1993.
yes_means: Aurora's sales tax rises 0.129% starting Jan 1, 2027 and the city may borrow up to $105 million for community facilities.
no_means: No new tax for community facilities; Aurora's sales tax rate stays the same.
current_law: Aurora's city sales tax has not increased since 1993. Combined rate today: 8.5% in the Adams County part of Aurora, 8% in the Arapahoe County part. A city task force identified $2.08 billion in infrastructure needs and narrowed to 65 projects costing $264.5 million.
fiscal_impact: Up to $12.64 million a year (DSA figure) and up to $105 million in bonds through 2057 (Kim Monson's summary of the ballot title). If all three pass, Aurora's combined sales tax goes to 8.825% (Adams side) or 8.325% (Arapahoe side).
confusing_wording_note: 3A, 3B and 3C are separate yes/no votes that look like one package. You can vote yes on some and no on others. Each includes bond authority through 2057 that the short description does not mention.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say the three measures address long-deferred infrastructure needs identified by a citizen task force, and that Aurora has not raised its sales tax in more than 30 years. Denver DSA backs 3A as 'an investment in our community.'

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson's conservative guide recommends NO on all three, citing a new tax with 30-year bonds. Protesters at council meetings objected mainly to the police portion (3B), not 3A.

official_title: Shall the City of Aurora raise the sales and use tax by 0.064% starting on Jan. 1, 2027, to provide for public safety needs, including without limitation the operation, repair, maintenance and improvements to police, fire and other public safety infrastructure and facilities... (as quoted by the Denver Gazette)
plain_summary: A new 0.064% Aurora sales tax (about 6 cents on $100) from 2027 through 2057, and up to $53 million in bonds, for fire stations, 911 and police facilities.
yes_means: Aurora's sales tax rises 0.064% starting Jan 1, 2027 and the city may borrow up to $53 million for public safety facilities.
no_means: No new tax for public safety facilities.
current_law: See 3A. Aurora police operate under a state consent decree.
fiscal_impact: Up to $6.27 million a year (DSA figure) and up to $53 million in bonds through 2057.
confusing_wording_note: Same package note as 3A. This is the only one of the three that funds police facilities; the ballot title says 'police, fire and other public safety.'

supporters_case.text: Supporters say the measures address the $900 million in public safety facility needs identified by the task force.

opponents_case.text: Protesters at Aurora council meetings said they understand the need for infrastructure but 'don't want police projects funded.' Denver DSA recommends NO, citing the department's consent decree and a recent roughly 41% officer raise.

official_title: Shall the City of Aurora raise the sales and use tax rate by 0.132% beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, to provide for transportation infrastructure needs, including without limitation the operation of and repairs, maintenance and improvements to city transportation infrastructure and facilities... (as quoted by the Denver Gazette)
plain_summary: A new 0.132% Aurora sales tax (about 13 cents on $100) from 2027 through 2057, and up to $108 million in bonds, for roads, bridges, intersections and pedestrian safety.
yes_means: Aurora's sales tax rises 0.132% starting Jan 1, 2027 and the city may borrow up to $108 million for transportation.
no_means: No new tax for transportation.
current_law: See 3A. The task force identified $596 million in transportation needs.
fiscal_impact: Up to $12.94 million a year (DSA figure) and up to $108 million in bonds through 2057.
confusing_wording_note: Same package note as 3A.

supporters_case.text: Supporters cite intersection and pedestrian safety improvements, major bridge replacements and roadway expansion. Denver DSA backs it for the pedestrian safety and bridge work.

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson's guide recommends NO, citing a new tax with bonds through 2057. No organized opposition found.

plain_summary: Moves Aurora's regular city elections (mayor and council) from odd-numbered years to even-numbered years, when turnout is much higher, with one-time shortened terms to make the switch.
yes_means: Aurora city elections move to even years; some current terms are shortened once to line up the calendar.
no_means: Aurora keeps electing its mayor and council in odd-numbered years.
current_law: Aurora holds regular municipal elections in November of odd years (most recently November 2025).
fiscal_impact: Likely saves money by combining with state and federal elections; no official figure captured.
confusing_wording_note: The title (as summarized) reads as a 'direction' to move elections. Check the full charter language on Aurora's site for how terms are shortened and which seats are affected.

supporters_case.text: Denver DSA calls it 'the most consequential of the Aurora ballot measures' because even-year turnout is far higher, and says it could save money. Kim Monson's conservative guide also recommends YES.

opponents_case.text: No organized opposition found. Critics of such changes elsewhere argue local issues get buried under federal races on a long ballot.

official_title: SHALL CITY OF LAKEWOOD TAXES BE INCREASED BY UP TO $17,600,000 IN THE FIRST FULL FISCAL YEAR (COMMENCING JANUARY 1, 2027) AND BY WHATEVER ADDITIONAL AMOUNTS AS ARE RAISED ANNUALLY IN EACH SUBSEQUENT YEAR, THROUGH THE IMPOSITION OF AN ADDITIONAL SALES AND USE TAX OF 0.5% (INCREASING CITY'S SALES AND USE TAX RATE FROM THREE PERCENT (3%) TO THREE AND A HALF PERCENT (3.5%)), PROVIDED THAT: FOOD, AS DEFINED IN LAKEWOOD MUNICIPAL CODE SECTION 3.01.430 (WHICH INCLUDES GROCERIES), SHALL BE EXEMPT FROM SUCH ADDITIONAL HALF-PERCENT SALES AND USE TAX, AND SHALL THE TAX REVENUES FROM SUCH ADDITIONAL HALF PERCENT SALES TAX BE USED ONLY FOR THE FOLLOWING SPECIFIC PURPOSES: PUBLIC SAFETY PURPOSES, INCLUDING INVESTING IN CRIME PREVENTION AND HOMELESSNESS RESPONSE; AND TRAFFIC SAFETY IMPROVEMENTS, INCLUDING MAINTENANCE AND CONSTRUCTION OF STREETS AND SIDEWALKS, ROAD IMPROVEMENTS TO REDUCE VEHICLE SPEEDS, AND PEDESTRIAN AND BICYCLE SAFETY ENHANCEMENTS...
plain_summary: Raises Lakewood's city sales tax from 3% to 3.5% starting Jan 1, 2027 (groceries exempt), raising up to $17.6 million in the first year, restricted to crime prevention, homelessness response, sidewalks, street maintenance, traffic calming, and bike and pedestrian safety. Lakewood's first sales tax increase in 20 years.
yes_means: Lakewood's sales tax rises half a percent (not on groceries) and the money goes to a dedicated fund for the listed safety and street purposes.
no_means: Lakewood's sales tax stays at 3%.
current_law: Lakewood's city sales tax has been 3% for 20 years. Food is already exempt from city sales tax.
fiscal_impact: Up to $17.6 million in the first full year, growing with sales. Revenue goes to a dedicated fund with annual external audits.
confusing_wording_note: 'Public safety purposes' sounds like police funding. The Yes campaign and DSA both say the money is for crime prevention, homelessness outreach, mental health crisis response and lighting, and that policing and enforcement are 'intentionally and explicitly not included.' Read the ballot text: it does not say 'police.'

supporters_case.text: Our Lakewood (Yes on 2G) says at current funding it would take 200 years to finish Lakewood's missing sidewalks, that groceries stay exempt, and that Lakewood will still have one of the lowest sales tax rates in the area. Jeffco Dems and Denver DSA support.

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson's guide recommends NO as a new tax. No organized opposition committee found; the city collected statements for and against through an online form.

official_title: Shall Section 2.6(a) of the Lakewood Home Rule Charter regarding terms of office of the Mayor and City Councilmembers be amended to specify that the term of a newly elected Mayor or City Councilmember begins at the first regular meeting following certification of the results of the regular municipal election?
plain_summary: Housekeeping charter change: new mayors and council members take office at the first regular meeting after election results are certified.
yes_means: Terms start at the first regular meeting after certification.
no_means: The charter's current start-of-term wording stays.
fiscal_impact: None.
confusing_wording_note: Not confusing; a technical fix.

official_title: Shall Section 12.12 of the Lakewood Home Rule Charter be repealed and replaced, to repeal obsolete language authorizing an annual property tax increase of up to 7% without voter approval, and to replace that provision with language stating that the City must comply with the Colorado Constitution and may not increase property taxes without approval of the City's electors?
plain_summary: Deletes old charter language that let the city raise property taxes up to 7% a year without a vote (already overridden by TABOR) and replaces it with a plain statement that property tax increases need voter approval.
yes_means: The obsolete 7% clause is removed and the charter says property tax increases require a public vote.
no_means: The outdated clause stays in the charter (TABOR already blocks its use).
current_law: TABOR (Colorado Constitution Article X, Section 20) already requires voter approval for tax increases, so the 7% clause has been unusable since 1992.
fiscal_impact: None.
confusing_wording_note: A YES vote tightens the rule in writing; it does not create a new tax. Some voters read 'repealed and replaced' as loosening it.

official_title: Shall Sections 13.1(d) and 13.2(e) of the Lakewood Home Rule Charter regarding initiative and referendum procedures be amended to extend the time frame for conducting regular or special elections on initiative ordinances and referendums to not less than sixty (60) days and not more than one hundred fifty (150) days after the final determination of petition sufficiency?
plain_summary: Changes the window for holding a vote on a citizen initiative or referendum to 60 to 150 days after petition signatures are verified.
yes_means: The election window becomes 60 to 150 days after petitions are found sufficient.
no_means: The current charter timeline stays.
fiscal_impact: None stated.
confusing_wording_note: Kim Monson's guide reads this as giving the city more time to delay a citizen vote; supporters frame it as aligning with state election calendars. The ballot does not say what the current window is.

jurisdiction: Arvada Fire Protection District (most of Arvada)
official_title: SHALL ARVADA FIRE PROTECTION DISTRICT TAXES BE INCREASED BY $23,100,000 THE FIRST FISCAL YEAR, BEGINNING JANUARY 1, 2027, AND BY SUCH AMOUNTS AS ARE RAISED ANNUALLY THEREAFTER, BY A SALES TAX OF 1.0% (ONE PERCENT) EXCLUDING ON SALES OF FOOD FOR DOMESTIC HOME CONSUMPTION, PRESCRIPTION MEDICINES, DIAPERS, SCHOOL ACTIVITIES AND ALL OTHER CATEGORIES EXEMPT FROM STATE SALES TAX COLLECTIONS, FOR THE PURPOSES OF PROVIDING FIRE PROTECTION, AMBULANCE, EMERGENCY MEDICAL RESPONSE, RESCUE, SAFETY, AND SUPPORT SERVICES...
plain_summary: A new 1% sales tax (groceries, prescriptions and diapers exempt) for the Arvada Fire Protection District, raising about $23.1 million in the first year for firefighter and paramedic staffing, vehicles and stations. This is the fire district, not the City of Arvada; Arvada has no city measures this year.
yes_means: A 1% fire district sales tax starts Jan 1, 2027.
no_means: No new fire district sales tax.
current_law: The district is funded mainly by property tax today.
fiscal_impact: $23.1 million in year one, growing with sales.
confusing_wording_note: Numbered 6C and labeled 'Arvada Fire Protection District,' so some voters think it is a city tax. It is not. Also note the West Metro Fire district (Lakewood area) has its own 0.75% sales tax, 7C, on the same ballot.

supporters_case.text: The district says the money maintains firefighter and paramedic staffing and modernizes equipment and stations. Jeffco Dems support.

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson's guide recommends NO. No organized opposition found.

jurisdiction: Jeffco Public Schools (Jefferson County School District R-1, incl. Lakewood, Arvada, Golden)
official_title: SHALL JEFFERSON COUNTY SCHOOL DISTRICT R-1 TAXES BE INCREASED $73 MILLION IN 2026 FOR COLLECTION IN 2027, AND BY SUCH AMOUNTS IN SUBSEQUENT YEARS THAT WILL PRODUCE, WHEN COMBINED WITH PRIOR MILL LEVY OVERRIDE AMOUNTS, UP TO THE LIMIT ESTABLISHED FOR THE DISTRICT BY SECTION 22-54-108(3)(B)(VI), C.R.S.... ATTRACTING AND KEEPING HIGH-QUALITY STAFF BY RAISING COMPENSATION CLOSER TO THE MARKET AVERAGE... CAREER AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION PROGRAMS...
plain_summary: A $73 million a year property tax increase (mill levy override) for Jeffco Public Schools, mainly to raise teacher and staff pay toward the metro average, plus career and technical education. Costs the median Jeffco homeowner (about $632,000 home) roughly $145 a year.
yes_means: Jeffco school property taxes rise $73 million a year starting with 2027 collections.
no_means: No new override revenue; the district says it would face more cuts.
current_law: Jeffco cut $40 million and 350 positions in September 2026. The district says it ranks 9th of 10 metro districts for midpoint teacher salary.
fiscal_impact: $73 million in the first year; about $3.50 per month per $100,000 of home value for 5A and 5B combined ($145 a year for 5A alone on the median home).
confusing_wording_note: 5A and 5B are separate votes. 5A is for operating costs (pay); 5B is for buildings and technology. 'Up to the limit established by Section 22-54-108' means later years can rise to the state cap, not just $73 million.

supporters_case.text: The district says pay is not competitive with neighboring districts and teachers are leaving, raising class sizes. A citizens' committee would review spending. Jeffco Dems, JCEA (teachers union), JESPA and Denver DSA support.

opponents_case.text: Tom Coyne (notyetjeffco.org) argues 89% of the 2018 bond projects ran over budget, that raises should be tied to student performance, and that the district has not earned public trust. Kim Monson recommends NO.

jurisdiction: Jeffco Public Schools (Jefferson County School District R-1)
official_title: SHALL JEFFERSON COUNTY SCHOOL DISTRICT R-1 TAXES BE INCREASED $60 MILLION IN 2026 FOR COLLECTION IN 2027, AND ANNUALLY THEREAFTER AND UTILIZED FOR THE PURPOSES AUTHORIZED AND IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 22-54-108.7, C.R.S. (THE DEBT FREE SCHOOLS ACT)... CAPITAL CONSTRUCTION, TECHNOLOGY AND MAINTENANCE...
plain_summary: A $60 million a year property tax (a 'special purpose mill levy' under the Debt Free Schools Act) for Jeffco school building repairs: roofs, plumbing, heating and cooling, security and technology. Adjusts for inflation. Costs the median homeowner about $120 a year.
yes_means: Jeffco school property taxes rise $60 million a year for building and technology needs, pay-as-you-go rather than bonds.
no_means: No new building levy.
current_law: Jeffco last passed a bond in 2018. The Debt Free Schools Act lets districts levy for capital needs without borrowing.
fiscal_impact: $60 million in year one, inflation-adjusted after; about $120 a year on the median home.
confusing_wording_note: Unlike a bond, this tax does not end when a project is paid off; it continues and rises with inflation. The district publishes a 'facilities explorer' site showing needs.

supporters_case.text: The district says deferred maintenance risks 'catastrophic' failures and shows every identified deficiency online. Jeffco Dems support.

opponents_case.text: Opponents cite the 2018 bond's cost overruns and affordability. Kim Monson recommends NO.

plain_summary: A $10.3 million a year property tax increase (mill levy override) for Littleton Public Schools for teacher pay, career and technical education and school security. The district entered 2026-27 with a $10.6 million gap. Costs about $25 a year per $100,000 of home value, about $150 a year on a $600,000 home. Caps future increases at one mill a year.
yes_means: LPS property taxes rise $10.3 million a year starting with 2027 collections.
no_means: No new override; the district has already frozen wages and scheduled a furlough day.
current_law: LPS cut central office staff, froze wages and scheduled a districtwide furlough day before referring the measure.
fiscal_impact: $10,289,724 in 2027; about $25 per $100,000 of home value per year.
confusing_wording_note: Numbered 4A, the same number as the Denver Public Schools measure, but a different district. Littleton (city) voters in LPS see this; Littleton residents in other districts do not.

supporters_case.text: The district cites state funding formula changes, declining enrollment and rising costs.

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson recommends NO. No organized opposition found.

plain_summary: Charter change: a Thornton council member, including the mayor, gives up their seat when they formally declare candidacy for any other elected office (a 'resign to run' rule).
yes_means: Council members and the mayor must resign on declaring for another office.
no_means: No resign-to-run rule.
fiscal_impact: None.
confusing_wording_note: Summary only; full text not captured. Check Thornton's city clerk page.

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson recommends YES; no organized opposition found.

plain_summary: Lets Westminster Public Schools collect the full mill levy override amounts voters approved in 1988, 2002 and 2018, up to the state limit; supporters say about $2 million more a year. Only Westminster residents inside Westminster Public Schools (Adams County) vote on it.
yes_means: The district may collect up to its state override limit under past approvals.
no_means: Override collections stay where they are.
fiscal_impact: About $2 million more a year by supporters' figures.
confusing_wording_note: Another '4A' (Denver, Littleton and Westminster each have one). Summary only; full text not captured.

opponents_case.text: Kim Monson recommends NO; no organized opposition found.
